read: partial: pp.1-9 (abstract, introduction, related work, dataset construction and overview, evaluation setup, results, attention analysis, conclusion) read in full; Appendix A (curriculum, template creation, translation; pp.14-17) and E (robustness of the step-level judge, pp.24-25) read; the remaining appendices and prompt tables skimmed.
venue_now: arXiv 2606.08034v2 [cs.CV], 26 Sep 2026 (page 1 stamp; header 'Preprint'); no venue
what_it_is: Sci-rho is a dynamic, visually grounded STEM benchmark at Cambridge IGCSE and A-level: 606 Python templates in mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and computer science, each written by a STEM graduate, advanced undergraduate or olympiad medalist and cross-checked, that generate the problem image, the statement, step-by-step LaTeX solutions and the computed answer (pp.1-5, 15-16). Statements are machine-translated into six further languages and verified by native speakers, and ten instances per template per language give 42,420 instances (pp.4-5). Seventeen VLMs are scored on final answers within 1% tolerance, as average-case and worst-case accuracy over a template's variants; five of them are also scored on step recall, precision and F1 by a GPT-5.4 judge against the gold steps (pp.5-7). Worst-case accuracy falls 10-28 points below average accuracy for the closed models (p.7).
domain: visually grounded school and pre-university STEM (mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, computer science) in seven languages; not engineering
size: 606 templates (199 mathematics, 195 physics, 137 chemistry, 52 computer science, 23 biology) x 7 languages x 10 instances = 42,420 instances (pp.4-5); 17 VLMs, five of them in the step-level evaluation (pp.1, 7)
source_of_items: expert-written Python templates: about 38% original problems, the rest adapted from open sources, mostly Cambridge IGCSE and A-level past papers and earlier benchmarks (pp.3, 5)
instances: generated (numerical, pattern, colour, shape and function-type variants; at least ten per template; p.5)
has_gold_traces: yes: each instance comes with step-by-step LaTeX solutions generated by its template, written by the contributors with LLM help to turn the Python computation into LaTeX, and checked by reviewers (pp.4, 15-16)
evaluation: final answer within 1% tolerance, reported as average-case and worst-case accuracy across a template's variants (p.5); step-level recall, precision and F1, and worst-case step F1, from binary judgments by an LLM judge (GPT-5.4) that compares model steps with the gold steps (p.6)
human_validation: Items: contributors cross-validated each other's templates and a quality-control team checked the generated outputs, including intermediate steps and answers (pp.4, 16); translations were verified by native speakers, with 40 deliberately planted errors used to check the translators (p.4). Evaluator: none; the step judge (GPT-5.4, which also judges its own outputs) is checked only by re-judging GPT-5.4's outputs with Gemini 2.5 Pro (pp.24-25).
contamination_measures: generated instances and worst-case accuracy across variants (pp.1, 5); variables are drawn with a predetermined seed, so instances are reproducible rather than private (pp.15-16)

engtrace_use.explanation: Not cited in the May paper. Paragraph: physical sciences, or the introduction's sentence on symbolic templates beside GSM-Symbolic. It is built the way EngTrace is (expert-written Python templates that generate instances with reference steps and computed answers), and it takes its step precision and recall from EngTrace (cited as Gull et al., 2026, p.6), so it is the closest construction outside engineering and a reviewer may expect it to be acknowledged. It appeared after EngTrace's arXiv version (reference list), so it does not affect priority. What EngTrace must say it adds: Sci-rho is school-level and multimodal rather than engineering; its step scores come from an LLM judge with no human validation (pp.6, 24-25), whereas EngTrace checks milestones and arithmetic deterministically and validates its residual judge against experts; and its seeds are fixed and the instances reproducible, whereas EngTrace's pool is drawn from a private seed.

suggested_wording: Sci-rho (Azmi et al., 2026) extends symbolic templates to visually grounded school-level STEM problems in seven languages, generating 42,420 instances with reference steps from 606 Python templates, though its step-level scores come from an LLM judge.
facts_to_cite: 606 problem templates in mathematics (199), physics (195), chemistry (137), computer science (52) and biology (23) at Cambridge IGCSE and A-level, translated into seven languages (pp.1, 3-5).

Each template is a Python class written by STEM graduates, advanced undergraduates or olympiad medalists (eight people in all) that generates at least ten instances with images, step-by-step solutions and computed answers; ten instances per template per language give 42,420 instances (pp.4-5, 15).
About 38% of the problems are original; the rest are adapted from open sources, mostly Cambridge past papers and earlier benchmarks (pp.3, 5).
Variation types: numerical, pattern, colour, shape and function type (p.5).
Final answers are scored within 1% tolerance, as average-case and worst-case accuracy across a template's variants (p.5).

Step recall, precision and F1 are judged by GPT-5.4 against the gold steps for five of the 17 models; re-judging GPT-5.4's outputs with Gemini 2.5 Pro leaves the gap between average and worst-case step F1 wide (13.0-20.8 points with GPT-5.4, 15.5-25.0 with Gemini 2.5 Pro) (pp.6-7, 24-25).
Worst-case accuracy falls 10-28 points below average accuracy for the closed models, and further for smaller open models (p.7).
Variables are sampled with a predetermined seed, so every instance is reproducible (pp.15-16).
Its step-level precision and recall are 'inspired by' Xie et al. (2026) and Gull et al. (2026), i.e. EngTrace (p.6).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: generated instances from expert-written code templates with computed answers and reference steps (pp.4, 15-16); step-level precision and recall adopted from EngTrace (p.6); worst-case evaluation across variants (p.5); human review of templates (p.16). Lacks: engineering content (school-level STEM); deterministic step checks (GPT-5.4 judge, p.6); human validation of the step judge (pp.24-25); a private seed (p.16). It adds images and six non-English languages, which EngTrace lacks.
notes: Paragraph: physical sciences (or the introduction). The paper's name is Sci- followed by the Greek letter rho ('Science Rhobustness', p.1); this file writes 'Sci-rho' to stay plain ASCII. (1) The abstract's '4,242 problem templates (606 per language)' counts language versions: there are 606 distinct templates (pp.1, 4); the search note's '4,242 expert-written Python templates' overstates it. (2) Confirmed from the text: it cites EngTrace's arXiv version (Gull et al., 2026, arXiv 2511.01650) as inspiration for step recall and precision (p.6 and references). (3) The step-level evaluation covers 5 of the 17 models, for budget reasons (p.7). (4) Should rather than must: it follows EngTrace, sits outside engineering, and a reviewer is unlikely to treat its omission as a gap; the consolidator may raise it if the revision makes any claim about template benchmarks with gold steps. (5) Like LPDS and ERI it cites EngTrace by its authors' names, so the anonymous ARR version should acknowledge it in the third person.
